lead: A circuit is a network of three ideal elements: resistance, inductance and capacitance. Each one is completely described by one fixed relation between its voltage and current. That relation tells you what the element does at every instant, including after a long time when nothing changes. A resistor keeps a voltage drop, an inductor becomes a short, a capacitor becomes an open. The same three rules model a heater coil, a transformer winding and the capacitor inside a fan regulator.

blocks.text: Charge Q is quantity of electricity, in coulombs (C). One coulomb is the charge of about 6.24 × 10¹⁸ electrons. Current is the rate of flow of charge: I = dQ/dt, where I is current in amperes (A), Q is charge in coulombs, t is time in seconds. One ampere is one coulomb per second.

blocks.where: V is voltage in volts (V); W is energy in joules (J); Q is charge in coulombs (C). One volt is one joule per coulomb.

blocks.text: Voltage is energy per unit charge. Power is the rate of energy transfer: P = VI, where P is power in watts (W), V is voltage in volts, I is current in amperes. Energy is the integral of power over time, E = ∫P dt, in joules. In a DC circuit the quantities are constant, so E = Pt and I = Q/t for steady flow. These four quantities describe any two-terminal element without knowing what is inside it.

sections.h3: Resistor, inductor, capacitor: one rule each

blocks.text: An ideal resistor obeys v = iR at every instant. Here v is voltage across the resistor in volts, i is current through it in amperes, R is resistance in ohms (Ω). It converts electrical energy to heat and stores none. Its power is P = vi = i²R = v²/R.

An ideal inductor obeys v = L di/dt. L is inductance in henry (H); di/dt is the rate of change of current in A/s. If current is constant, di/dt = 0, so v = 0: in DC steady state the inductor is a short circuit. It stores magnetic energy ½Li².

An ideal capacitor obeys i = C dv/dt. C is capacitance in farad (F); dv/dt is the rate of change of voltage in V/s. If voltage is constant, dv/dt = 0, so i = 0: in DC steady state the capacitor is an open circuit. It stores electric energy ½Cv².

These rules are the whole element. A 5 Ω resistor is not “a resistor plus something else” in the lumped model; its rule is v = 5i. The same applies to L and C. Real components have small extra effects, but the ideal rule is the exam model.

An element is linear if its v-i graph is a straight line through the origin. A constant resistance is linear. A filament lamp is non-linear because its resistance rises as it heats. An element is passive if it cannot deliver net energy to the rest of the circuit; R, L and C are passive. Ideal voltage and current sources are active; for those see independent and dependent sources.

In the lumped model, each element’s property is concentrated at one point and the wires are ideal. A real coil has both L and R; a real capacitor has some leakage R. At 50 Hz these extra effects are small, so the lumped model works. At high frequency, a wire itself behaves as a distributed element. Only a few universities teach the lumped/distributed distinction formally.

figure.caption: Each element’s rule drives its long-time DC behaviour: the resistor keeps a voltage drop, the inductor becomes a short, the capacitor an open. All three arrows end at the same steady-state block; only the label on the arrow changes.

spec.title: v-i relation decides DC behaviour
spec.aria: Three element blocks — resistor, inductor, capacitor — each pointing down to the same DC steady-state block, labelled no change, short and open.

examples.question: A 10 V DC source is connected in series with a 5 Ω resistor and one unknown element. After a long time the circuit has settled to DC steady state. Find the current I, the voltage V_x across the unknown element and the energy E stored in it when the element is (a) a 5 Ω resistor, (b) a 2 H inductor, (c) a 2 mF capacitor. For (a) also give the power in the unknown resistor.
steps: After a long time the circuit is in DC steady state: all currents and voltages are constant. So di/dt = 0 for any inductor and dv/dt = 0 for any capacitor.
(a) The unknown element is 5 Ω. Total resistance = 5 + 5 = 10 Ω. I = 10/10 = 1 A. V_x = I × 5 = 1 × 5 = 5 V. P = I²R = 1² × 5 = 5 W. A resistor stores no energy: E = 0 J.
(b) An inductor is a short in DC steady state, so V_x = 0 V. The only resistance is 5 Ω. I = 10/5 = 2 A. E = ½Li² = ½ × 2 × 2² = 4 J.

(c) A capacitor is an open in DC steady state, so I = 0 A. No current flows in the 5 Ω resistor, so its drop is 0 V. The full source voltage appears across the capacitor: V_x = 10 V. E = ½Cv² = ½ × 2×10⁻³ × 10² = 0.1 J.
examples.answer: The results are (a) I = 1 A, V_x = 5 V, P = 5 W, E = 0 J; (b) I = 2 A, V_x = 0 V, E = 4 J; (c) I = 0 A, V_x = 10 V, E = 0.1 J.

traps: After a long time, an inductor is a short circuit (0 V), not an open circuit. A capacitor is an open circuit (0 A), not a short circuit.
Use i²R or v²/R with the voltage across that resistor, not the source voltage, when other elements are in series.
Convert prefixes before calculating: 2 mF = 2 × 10⁻³ F, not 2 × 10⁻⁶ F; 2 H stays 2 H.
Do not swap the stored-energy formulas: inductor energy is ½Li², capacitor energy is ½Cv².
An ideal resistor stores no energy even though it dissipates power; that power becomes heat.

quiz.q: State the v-i relation and the unit of an ideal inductor.
quiz.a: v = L di/dt, with L in henry (H).

quiz.q: Which ideal element is a short circuit in DC steady state, and which is an open circuit?
quiz.a: Inductor is a short; capacitor is an open.

quiz.q: Why does an ideal resistor store zero energy even though it dissipates power?
quiz.a: It converts electrical energy to heat at the moment of flow; it does not store energy in an electric or magnetic field.

quiz.q: A 12 V source, a 3 Ω resistor and a 4 H inductor are in series. After a long time, find the current and the energy stored in the inductor.
quiz.a: Inductor is a short, so I = 12/3 = 4 A. E = ½ × 4 × 4² = 32 J.

quiz.q: A 2 mF capacitor has 50 V across it. Find its charge and stored energy.

A coil is modelled as 5 Ω in series with 2 H. After a long time it draws 2 A from a DC source. Find the source voltage and the energy stored. If the coil is replaced by a 2 mF capacitor, find the steady current.
quiz.a: Inductor is short, so source voltage = 2 × 5 = 10 V. E = ½ × 2 × 2² = 4 J. Capacitor is open, so steady current = 0 A.

quiz.q: A filament lamp has 10 V across it at 0.5 A, and 20 V across it at 0.8 A. Is it linear? Justify with resistance values.
quiz.a: R = 10/0.5 = 20 Ω at the first point; R = 20/0.8 = 25 Ω at the second. Resistance is not constant, so the lamp is non-linear.

beyond: Not for the exam. In real hardware, every wire has small resistance and inductance, and every pair of conductors has capacitance. At high frequency these parasitics dominate, so engineers use distributed models and field solvers. Supercapacitors and power inductors are chosen by stored energy and ripple current in converters and electric vehicles. Search next for “parasitic extraction”, “lumped versus distributed model” and “DC-DC converter energy storage”.
